Wounded by Love and jealous of a rival suitor or possible attendant, he uses deception to bind her: he writes a verse on an apple, causing her to pronounce an oath before Diana. In his letter he calls that single pledge sufficient, presents his ancestry and morals, asks Cydippe to reject her rival, and insists he seeks to be her husband rather than an adulterer. He petitions Diana for Cydippe’s welfare, fears for her affection and safety, and endures her anger, yet threatens force or further schemes if persuasion fails. Cydippe portrays his written oath as a distant wound that harms her, doubts his influence with Diana, but ultimately says she wishes to be united with him.

Cydippe is a maiden and virgin of marriageable age whose future is governed by an oath she unknowingly makes to Acontius. While traveling to Delos, she reads aloud the inscription on his apple without understanding its trap, thereby swearing before Diana to marry him. Although she is also intended for another husband in a marriage desired by her parents, she becomes bound to Acontius and fears Diana’s judgment if she breaks the pledge. Whenever marriage preparations arise, she suffers recurring illness, languor, wasting, fever, and weakness, and Hymenaeus flees her wedding rites. At first she protests that Acontius deceived an inexperienced girl and gained no glory by doing so; she writes to him pale and barely able to finish her letter. Yet she blushes at the oath, confesses that she wants to join him, rejects the intended husband, and tells her mother the circumstances. Her nurse protects her by concealing correspondence and signaling visitors. Her course moves from unwitting entrapment and illness toward acknowledging the pledge and accepting Acontius as husband.
records.t: Cydippe is a maiden and virgin of marriageable age whose future is governed by an oath she unknowingly makes to Acontius. While traveling to Delos, she reads aloud the inscription on his apple without understanding its trap, thereby swearing before Diana to marry him. Although she is also intended for another husband in a marriage desired by her parents, she becomes bound to Acontius and fears Diana’s judgment if she breaks the pledge. Whenever marriage preparations arise, she suffers recurring illness—languor, wasting, fever, and weakness—and Hymenaeus flees her wedding rites. At first she protests that Acontius deceived an inexperienced girl and gained no glory by doing so; she writes to him pale and barely able to finish her letter. Yet she blushes at the oath, confesses that she wants to join him, rejects the intended husband, and tells her mother the circumstances. Her nurse protects her by concealing correspondence and signaling visitors. Her course moves from unwitting entrapment and illness toward acknowledging the pledge and accepting Acontius as husband.

records.s: Delos is a sacred island, stained with votive blood during sacrifice and visited by Cydippe. It contains Diana's lofty temple, other temples and porticoes, kings' gifts, statues, a horn-built altar, and the tree beside which the goddess gave birth; Cydippe recalls these holy sites and offerings.

Love is a cruel, powerful boy, Venus’s son and Mars’s stepson, with arrows, doves, and a chariot. It causes and strengthens Acontius’s passion, advises his binding of Cydippe through composed words, and sets nets for her. It also rules love poetry: interrupting an epic attempt, it steals a metrical foot, turns the work to elegy, shoots the speaker, and appears victorious with captives and attendants.

records.l: Cydippe's oath to Acontius, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Cydippe’s oath to Acontius is a disputed pledge of marriage made when Cydippe read aloud words on an apple Acontius threw to her in Diana’s temple. Acontius says Diana witnessed the binding oath and demands that Cydippe honor it rather than commit perjury. Cydippe argues that she did not swear freely: only deliberate intention makes words binding.

records.l: Cydippe and Acontius's marriage, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Cydippe and Acontius’s marriage is a promised but unfulfilled union. Acontius seeks marriage and pledged fidelity, claiming their oath binds Cydippe to him as her destined husband. As the marriage approaches, Cydippe’s illness repeatedly delays it; she questions whether her words were a deliberate promise that grants him marital rights.

Acontius’s letter is a second stratagem and evidence of his continued pursuit of Cydippe. It wounds the speaker from afar and contributes to her illness. Asking to be read so her illness may depart, it defends deception, invokes an oath, threatens further action, pleads for acceptance, and is answered by her confession that she wants union with him.

Cydippe’s illness is a persistent, unexplained languor that resists physicians and becomes severe whenever her marriage rites are prepared. It leaves her fevered, weak, wasted, bloodless, and pale, recurring as she attempts to evade a pledge. Its cause is disputed: some cite chance, divine disapproval, or Acontius’s arts, while Acontius says Diana sends it because Cydippe has broken her oath. He maintains that rejecting the rival suitor and honoring the pledge will restore her lasting health.

Acontius conceals a marriage oath on an apple and arranges for Cydippe to read it in Diana's temple, thereby ensnaring her without openly proposing. Cydippe condemns the attempted compulsion; Acontius admits deception, invokes love and union, calls his letter another stratagem, and threatens more.

causes violence against the mistress [by driving the lover to reckless blows] Anger makes the lover its prey and drives him to raise reckless hands against his mistress. Afterward, he recognizes that he used his strength against her and condemns his own anger.

Acontius’s apple is a rolling apple carrying a written oath and verse declaring his marriage claim. It comes or is thrown before Cydippe at Diana’s temple, where she reads its deceptive-looking but binding words in Diana’s presence and is caught into accepting the oath, nearly swearing again. Its bloodless color is compared with her pallor, and Acontius proposes a golden image at Delos as testimony that the inscription was fulfilled.

records.l: Cydippe's rival suitor, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Cydippe's rival suitor, promised her by her father, remains healthy while pursuing an unjust claim that causes her illness and danger; Acontius urges her to reject and bar him.

The letter urges Cydippe to fulfill her oath, explains the dangers of continued refusal, and tells her what to recount to her mother. Acontius closes it by asking her to act so that both of them may be safe.

records.l: the inscription on the apple, Heroides and Amores
records.s: An inscription presents Cydippe a marriage oath; read before Diana, it makes her blush and binds her to Acontius, though she says it forced or deceived her.

records.l: Cydippe's voyage to Delos, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Cydippe travelled by ship to Delos because she was eager to see the island, though the voyage began under an ill omen. She passed Myconos, Tenos, and Andros, reached Delos, and later visited its sacred places with her mother and nurse.

records.l: the rivalry between Acontius and Cydippe's suitor, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Acontius and Cydippe's suitor are engaged in a conflict in which neither yields and each believes the other is not his equal. Their rivalry obstructs both of their wishes, while Cydippe suffers the consequences.

is_a epistolary poem [in Ovid's Heroides] Heroides XXI is a letter in which a sick speaker addresses Acontius about his written oath, her failed marriages, Diana’s anger, and her eventual willingness to become his wife.

records.l: the written oath, Heroides and Amores
records.s: binds the speaker of Heroides XXI [through a written pledge] The written oath has bound the speaker despite her lack of genuine consent and has become the basis of her conflict with Acontius. She eventually yields to it and tells her mother about the pledge her tongue was trapped into giving.

records.l: the intended husband, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The intended husband honors the speaker’s virginity while sitting beside her, but her avoidance of touch, speech, and kisses makes him suspicious.
The Amores is a work of largely lighthearted love poems, featuring Corinna among several loves; it reflects Rome and Italy of its time and provides information on manuscripts and editions.

Corinna is a beautiful, celebrated, and haughty woman who is the speaker’s beloved and mistress, loved by Naso and Ovid and made the subject of verse. Her beauty is described as unmatched, but she lacks apparel or payment worthy of it; she knows the power of her appearance and gains pride from seeing herself in a mirror. She is watched by her husband, keeper, and guards, making access to her difficult, yet she also attracts wealthy lovers and is preferred by a newly rich soldier. Advice given around her urges the strategic use of modesty, rivals, refusals, and gifts. Her relationship with the speaker unfolds through desire, delays, jealousy, and public fame. She visits him at midday in a loose tunic, resists as he removes it, and they have sex before resting. At other times she hesitates to visit, sends tablets refusing him, keeps him out, and can renew his desire by feigning illness or wrongdoing before becoming affectionate. She is jealous of other women, especially Cypassis, and mourns her parrot, whose final word is her name. She suffers distress after losing her once abundant hair through her own treatment. She prepares for a dangerous sea voyage, and later undergoes a dangerous attempt to end a pregnancy, causing the speaker to fear for her life. Though Ovid says she first inspired his poetry, he fears his praise has made her common, known to many, and sexually available to others; another woman even claims the distinguished name Corinna because of that poetry.

Tibullus is a sacred bard and the glory of Elegy. He dies, is burned on a high funeral pyre, and is buried as ashes in an urn while his mother and sister mourn; Delia and Nemesis loved him. His fame endures, and he is imagined received in Elysium.

Love poetry is a light poetic form, suited to youthful subjects and the alternating six- and five-foot elegiac couplet, including The Amores. It begins when the speaker abandons violent epic after Cupid changes his meter, drawing its subject and lasting fame from the beloved woman. In the later account, Elegy and Cupid defend its power against Tragedy, and the poet continues it temporarily before a greater task.

records.l: P. Ovidius Naso, Heroides and Amores
records.s: P. Ovidius Naso is a poet, lover, and author of the Amores, revised from five booklets into three. In its episodes, the speaker suffers frustrated meetings, reproaches Aurora, comforts the beloved woman, and trusts poetry to preserve him after death. Recalling her apparent infidelity, he prays for death, threatens retaliation, then relents at her sorrow, asks for kisses, and remains jealous of a rival.

records.l: the poet's Amores, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A love-poetry work in elegiac couplets, now three booklets rather than five, presenting Cupid, Love, the speaker’s beloved woman, and Corinna.

records.l: the speaker's beloved woman's husband, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_married_to Corinna [he is her husband] The beloved woman's husband attends the same banquet as the speaker and the woman. The speaker fears his physical intimacy with her, instructs her to avoid his embraces and kisses, and hopes that wine will make him sleep so that the lovers can find an opportunity to meet.

Love is a ruling, cruel power that takes possession of the speaker after Cupid’s wounding, enslaves lovers, and is neither idle nor spiritless. It demands experience and energy, drives hardship and action, causes sleeplessness, and directs Ovid from epic subjects toward elegies. It also divides the speaker’s affection between two beautiful women, yet he chooses love’s trouble over solitude and imagines an erotic death. From initial torment and resistance, its burden becomes lighter when accepted; it then grows through refusal, fear, delay, and obstacles, while excess makes it cloying and harmful.

records.l: the husband-wife banquet, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The husband-wife banquet brings the speaker, Corinna, and Corinna’s husband together; amid the crowd, the speaker secretly directs Corinna through touches, looks, gestures, cups, and wine while forbidding affection for her husband.

Cupid's triumph is imagined as a sacred public victory procession over lovers: Cupid rides a golden dove-drawn chariot while captives, attendants, roses, and jewels follow, ending with the speaker's submission as newly captured prey.

records.l: the speaker's submission to Cupid, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_a submission [to Cupid's laws] The speaker confesses that he is Cupid's new prey and stretches out his hands to accept Cupid's laws. He asks for peace rather than war and accepts that his poetry must rise in six-foot lines and settle into five-foot lines.

The janitor, a door guardian at the mistress's threshold, is enslaved and chained. Iron-hearted toward the lover's pleas, he repeatedly refuses to open the door despite appeals to gratitude and threats, seeming suited to guard a gloomy prison.

is_a beautiful girl [whose threshold the janitor guards] The mistress is the lover's beloved and is inside the house whose door he cannot enter. In the later episode, she is frightened and wounded when the lover tears her hair and marks her cheeks, but she remains silent while her tears and expression accuse him.

A portal secured by a guardian and bar, braced with hard oak, stays closed and deaf to a lover’s tears, prayers, threats, and appeals. A seeming movement proves to be wind; the lover curses it and bids farewell to door and posts.
secures door [during the lover's vigil] The lover repeatedly orders the door bar to be removed before the night ends. It remains in place, braced by hard oak, and prevents him from entering.

is_long long [the janitor's burden of slavery] The chain binds the janitor, and the lover wishes that the janitor may eventually be freed from it and no longer have to drink the water of slavery. The chain is also invoked as a possible punishment for the lover's own violent hands.

encourages lover [with love and wine, toward lack of restraint] The night initially frightens the lover with darkness and empty phantoms, but Love makes him brave enough to travel and keep watch at the door. As the hours pass, the city becomes silent, dew falls, and dawn approaches while the door remains shut.

records.l: violence against the mistress, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Violence against the mistress is committed by the lover in madness: after threats and tearing her gown, he injures Corinna, whose fear and tears make him recognize his crime.

records.l: the lover's vigil at the door, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The lover spends the night outside the closed door, repeatedly calling for the bar to be removed and listening for signs that the door has opened. He sheds tears, wears a garland that falls from his hair, and remains outside until the approach of dawn, when he leaves the garland on the threshold as evidence of his miserable vigil.

Dipsas, whose thirst accords with her name, is an old bawd and practitioner of magic. Never sober in relation to Aurora, she knows Aeaean incantations and magic that can control clouds and day and summon dead ancestors. As a profaner of chaste union, she advises a young woman as a procurer, urging wealthy lovers, deception, rivalry, feigned feeling, and demands for gifts; the narrator overhears her.

records.l: the wealthy young lover, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A wealthy young lover, captivated by a young woman's face, desires her and can meet her needs; Dipsas urges her to profit from him while keeping him uncertain and jealous.

requires youth [the age suited to warfare is also suited to Venus] War is compared with love through their shared dangers, sleeplessness, watchfulness, sieges, attacks, and uncertain outcomes. The unit says that both war and love can bring down people who seemed impossible to defeat, while the defeated may rise again.

records.l: gifts and payment for sexual favors, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The topic is gifts and payment for sexual favors. Dipsas teaches a young woman to feign love, admit lovers according to their gifts, and use her slaves, sister, mother, and nurse to seek more, including through birthday pretexts, rivals' presents, and unrepaid loans; the narrator's poetry is deemed inadequate. The later account condemns payment as degrading and incompatible with love, distinguishing it from freely given gifts. It values a poor lover's service, devotion, faithfulness, and poetry, whose fame can outlast material gifts.
Isis is a goddess associated with Paraetonium, Canopus, Memphis, Pharos, and the Nile, invoked to attend to Corinna and grant her life, sparing her and the speaker.

The lover is a soldier in love: serving and guarding a mistress, watching rivals as enemies, and besieging her threshold. Former idleness becomes action under love. Suited to a spirit experienced in trials, the lover endures night, cold, rain, snow, mountains, rivers, and sea travel.

A warrior serves as a captain’s guard, keeping watch at the door and through the night. He endures long roads, harsh weather, and ground rest, scouts enemies, besieges cities, breaks gates, and embodies courage and endurance.
A woman who sells sexual access at a fixed price, the harlot is controlled by a greedy pander, curses that authority, and performs under compulsion for gain.

charges man [for mutual sexual pleasure] The woman is criticized for being the only creature said to demand payment for mutual sexual pleasure, to hire out her nights, and to profit from what both partners desire. The unit nevertheless says that a woman may properly request gifts from a wealthy person and that a poor lover should give whatever he has, including service, devotion, faithfulness, and poetry.

pays woman [for sexual pleasure] The man is presented as contributing to sexual pleasure together with the woman, yet being made to suffer a financial loss when the woman demands payment. A poor man is said to offer his service, devotion, faithfulness, and whatever possessions he has to his beloved.

is_mutual woman [shared by man and woman] Sexual pleasure is described as something that man and woman both enjoy and jointly produce. Because it is mutual, the unit questions why one person should sell it and the other should have to buy it.

Nape is a personal attendant, not a handmaid, skilled at arranging hair, giving signals, and aiding secret nighttime meetings. Faithful to Naso in trouble and touched by Cupid, she repeatedly urges Corinna to visit him. Naso ultimately entrusts her with tablets, asking her to secure Corinna’s response.

The wax tablets are double writing tablets with wax surfaces, inscribed by Naso and carried by Nape to Corinna as love correspondence. Naso asks Corinna for a reply, saying “Come!” would suffice and promising to dedicate them to Venus. They return bearing her refusal to come that day, provoking curses and wishes for their destruction.
A terse wax message asks Corinna to come secretly at night, saying Naso’s hope of seeing her keeps him alive and seeking a prompt reply.

records.l: secret nighttime meeting, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Nape is known for her usefulness in the service of a secret nighttime meeting and for giving signals. She has often encouraged Corinna to come to Naso, but the unit does not state that the meeting occurs.

Naso’s love correspondence with Corinna is carried through Nape and written on wax tablets. Naso wants Corinna’s written response to occupy the tablets rather than leave them largely blank, though he would accept the single-word reply “Come!”

The dawn ends the speaker’s night with the beloved woman even though sleep is still deep, the air cool, and the birds singing. Its arrival wakes travelers, soldiers, farmers, boys, lawyers, and women who work wool.

is_a fine and abundant bodily hair [formerly belonging to the beloved woman] The beloved woman’s former hair was abundant, delicate, easily arranged, and a mixture of black and golden color. It endured irons and fire but was ultimately ruined by her own dyes and treatments; the speaker says that replacement hair from captive German women will be sent.

Envy accuses the speaker of wasting his vigorous years and producing poetry instead of pursuing military prizes or legal work. The speaker says that Envy feeds on the living but becomes quiet after death.

records.l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Poetry and poetic fame are a powerful art that seeks lasting renown worldwide. Song can overcome natural and physical barriers, including barred doors, and earns the poet favor from his beloved mistress. It outlasts material achievements, rulers, wealth, monuments, and its creators, preserving named poets’ works and promising the speaker’s own survival through verse.

records.l: the beloved mistress, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A beloved woman initially closes her door to the poet, but song and poetry soften resistance; abandoning thunderbolt imagery for elegy, he gains her beauty, favor, and eventual return.

records.l: the mistress's guardian, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The mistress’s guardian is a eunuch who strictly blocks Ovid’s access to the beloved mistress. Unable to share mutual sexual love, he is urged to accept gifts, gain honor and savings through silence, permit secret meetings, and avoid punishment for exposing an affair.

The husband is Corinna’s jealous judge in accusations of adultery, yet is influenced by his beloved mistress and fails to guard her from the speaker. Criticized as slow and overly tolerant, he is urged to shut doors, investigate visitors and messages, and recognize her estrangement; his indulgence enables the affair and threatens the speaker’s possession of her.

is excessive vigilance [toward a mistress] Excessive guardianship is presented as provoking hatred and making illicit love more desirable. Ovid argues that surveillance damages the husband, mistress, and guardian, while a guardian who keeps silent gains influence, rewards, and eventual freedom.

The beloved girl, the speaker/lover’s mistress, secretly communicates with and kisses a rival despite shared kisses and instruction in kissing; confronted, she blushes and seems sorrowful, then gives the speaker/lover exceptionally pleasing kisses.

Love is a painful yet desired force: it makes the speaker pray for death, suffer jealousy over the beloved girl’s kisses, and feel physically weakened. It repeatedly draws him back into its wars and familiar weapons even when desire cools, while its uncertain pleasures and rejections outweigh peaceful rest. By the end, love affects mortals and gods alike and overcomes the speaker’s hatred of the beloved woman’s faults through her beauty.

The beloved girl’s infidelity is revealed not by intercepted letters or gifts but by the speaker/lover’s direct observation of her secret signs and kisses with another man. The speaker/lover considers his case against her overwhelmingly strong, yet wishes he could be unable to win it.

Jealousy makes the speaker/lover angry when he sees the beloved girl kissing another man, but it also torments him after she gives him better and seemingly newly learned kisses. He fears that the rival has tasted the same pleasures and wishes the rival’s kisses had not been equally satisfying.
Kisses shared with the beloved girl are intimate; after another man apparently teaches her, her kisses to the speaker become heartfelt, powerful, and more skillful.

The parrot comes from India and is prized for rare beauty, a Punic-red and saffron beak, human-voice mimicry, peaceful companionship, and a frugal diet of nuts, poppy-seeds, and water. After dying, it bids Corinna farewell, is mourned by birds and Corinna, joins pious birds in Elysium, and receives a body-sized tomb.
turtle-dove, a friendly, faithful bird, lives harmoniously as parrot’s companion, remains loyal through their shared life’s end, and is urged to grieve first.

Cypassis is Corinna’s skilled, faithful female servant and hairdresser. Accused of sharing Corinna’s couch with the speaker, she is first denied by him, then revealed as his secret partner; he threatens to expose their meetings if she refuses him.

records.l: the speaker's beloved, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A fair lady loved by Ovid receives and wears a welcome ring. The speaker imagines her touching herself, bathing, and sealing secret tablets with it, then urges her to come quickly by small carriage if she cares for him.

records.l: Cypassis and the speaker's affair, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_secret stolen delight [between the speaker and Cypassis] The affair is a secret sexual relationship between Cypassis and the speaker. Although the speaker denies the accusation when defending himself to Corinna, he later refers openly to their previous encounters and uses knowledge of them to pressure Cypassis into another meeting.

records.l: two simultaneous love affairs, Heroides and Amores
records.s: are_experienced_by the speaker [at the same time] The speaker admits that he loves two women at the same time, despite having previously denied that this was possible. He presents this condition as shameful but acknowledges that he has been caught loving both simultaneously.
Corinna's voyage is a dangerous sea journey from home, exposed to adverse winds and storms; the speaker fears for her, urges her return, and hopes to welcome her safe escape.

has_as_spoil Corinna [captured by the speaker's strategy] The speaker claims a triumph because Corinna is in his arms after being guarded by her husband, keeper, and door. He calls it a special victory because it was won without bloodshed or military assistance, with himself serving as commander, soldier, cavalry, infantry, and standard-bearer.
Ilia, a Trojan descendant and Vestal, suffers distress from her uncle's crime and Mars's wrongdoing, fears disgrace, drowns herself in Anio's waters, and becomes Anio's wife.
Pregnancy is a hidden bodily burden that endangers Corinna; as she struggles to deliver, a speaker fearing responsibility begs Isis and Ilithyia to save her.

Abortion is condemned as self-destructive violence: women wound themselves and poison unborn children to avoid bodily marks, may die after destroying pregnancy, and are urged to let pregnancy reach natural maturity.

records.l: the unborn children, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The unborn children are vulnerable, tender lives in the womb, threatened by abortion, weapons, and deadly poisons; destroying them before birth prevents future people from existing.

A gift for the speaker’s fair beloved, the ring carries the giver’s love rather than material value. Sent to circle her finger, stay with her even in bathing, and seal secret letters, it becomes the speaker’s envied imagined means of touching her lips and bosom as a man.

Sulmo is a small, wholesome, fertile town in the Paelignian fields, watered by streams and enclosed by walls. It is Ovid’s hometown and the speaker’s setting; though its waters and fields are praised, it cannot please him while his beloved is distant.

records.l: Ovid's Paelignian homeland, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The Paelignian country is Ovid’s small, healthy, water-rich homeland, fertile in corn, grass, grain, grapes, olives, and the berry-bearing tree of Pallas. It begins as abundant, refreshed by streams and breezes; without the beloved it feels no longer healthy. Ovid then claims its people, their honorable arms, and his future glory.

records.l: the sea voyage and journey, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A speaker imagines a journey with his beloved: together they would cross the Alps, Libyan Syrtes, and dangerous seas without fearing Malea or Charybdis, and he would carry her if Neptune defeated their ship. It ends by contrasting Hero’s visitor’s failed, blinded route.

records.l: separation from the beloved, Heroides and Amores
records.s: separates Ovid [from the beloved] Separation places the speaker away from the woman who causes his passion. It makes Sulmo and his father's country seem like Scythia, the fierce Cilicians, the green Britons, and rocks reddened by Promethean blood. The beloved had sworn to remain his companion, but the speaker says that girls' promises are often carried away by wind and water.

records.l: love and longing, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The speaker's love is expressed through the gift of the ring and through his wish to become the object that touches and accompanies his beloved. His longing makes him envy his own gift and desire physical closeness with her. He asks her to turn her promises into actions by coming to him.

Beauty gives confidence, pride, and lasting privilege, even protecting a faithless girl from divine offense. Yet it breeds arrogance, jealous desire, and adultery; its possessors should not scorn lesser partners or let beauty promise rule.

The speaker values felicitous poems as more important than great wealth and says that many women want to acquire a name through his poetry. He declares that only his mistress will be sung in his books and that she alone will provide the cause for his poetic talent. Love redirects his poetry from epic and tragedy toward the art of love and letters written for legendary figures.

Elegy is a feminine, love-associated poetic genre personified as a graceful woman with uneven feet, thin robe, loving expression, and a myrtle branch. She inspires the poet, enables Corinna’s secret love, and defends her light Cupid-suited style, winning the poet’s continuation. She gives the poet’s love lasting renown, then mourns Tibullus with loosened hair and tears.

Tragedy is a Roman, exalted personified genre. She appears in a powerful stride with a royal sceptre and high Lydian buskin, reproaches the poet’s continual love writing, urges heroic poetry as greater work, then grants time for tender love poems.

records.l: woman at the races, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A woman attending circus races favors a charioteer while a poet beside her desires her, praises her appearance, seeks Venus’s aid, and reads her smile and eyes as promise of further favor.

A racing venue with assigned seating and a starting line, circus places the poet and woman close together, hosts four-horse chariot races and a gods’ procession, and lets its crowd demand restarts by waving togas.

uses horse team [four-horse teams] The chariot race begins when the praetor releases four-horse teams from equally placed starting barriers. The poet supports the charioteer favored by the woman, worries when he loses ground, and urges the crowd to call for a restart. After the second start, the favored charioteer wins, while the poet says that his own desired prize remains to be won.

records.l: the speaker’s beloved woman, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The speaker’s beloved is a tall, handsome, fair woman with rosy cheeks, small feet, and star-like eyes. Though accused of false oaths, repeated deception, rejecting the speaker, and taking other lovers, she remains beautiful and apparently unpunished. Her beauty sustains the speaker’s love, drawing him back despite resentment from beginning to end.

records.l: the hard husband, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A husband relies on surveillance, placing a keeper over his wife; told her will cannot be guarded, he is advised to abandon sternness and indulge her friends.

is_a woman [whose chastity cannot be produced by force] The wife cannot be made faithful merely by having her body guarded, since her mind may remain unfaithful. Her beauty and the husband's concern for her make her more desirable to other men, and she may bring many friends into his social circle.

records.l: the white heifer, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The shining white female heifer, the bull’s consort in a dream, bears a crow-pecked dark breast mark, then leaves him for bulls in richer pasture.

is_a bull [the white heifer's consort] The bull is the white heifer's happy mate and lies beside her while resting and chewing. After the heifer hesitates and leaves him, he is left on the abandoned bed.

records.l: the nocturnal dream augur, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A nocturnal dream augur interprets the speaker’s dream, identifying the white heifer as the beloved girl, the bull as the speaker, the crow as an old procuress, and the dark mark as evidence of adultery.

records.l: the dream vision, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The dream vision shows a grove, a green meadow, a white heifer with her bull, and a crow that pecks the heifer before she joins other bulls. Its interpretation presents the scene as a sign of the speaker's love, the girl's departure, and adultery.
Perjury occurs when the faithless girl breaks an oath sworn by her own eyes and by the speaker's eyes. The speaker complains that her perjury remains unpunished and that he suffers for it instead.

Divine punishment is shown as falling on men and on figures such as Semele, while beautiful women who swear falsely appear protected. The speaker questions whether the gods exist or whether they favor tender beautiful women.

records.l: guardianship of women, Heroides and Amores
records.s: fails_to_control the wife's will [even when every door is shut] Guardianship of women is presented as ineffective because a keeper can guard the body but not the will. The speaker says that strict custody provokes wrongdoing and that indulgence is a better way to influence a wife.

is_a desire for what is denied Forbidden desire makes people strive for what is denied and covet what is forbidden, like a sick person longing for prohibited water. The speaker uses the horse, Argus, Danae, and Penelope to show that restriction can intensify desire, while permission can weaken it.
Anio, a river god, sees grieving Ilia by his waters, rescues her from the river, offers refuge among his many nymphs, and marries her.

records.l: crossing the river, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_prevented_by the river's flood The crossing is difficult because the river has no bridge or boat and has grown far deeper than it was before. The narrator cannot reach the farther bank by any art and is forced to stand waiting.

records.l: Ilia's drowning and marriage to Anio, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_a mythic episode Ilia throws herself into the rushing waters after declaring that she would rather have died before becoming publicly disgraced. Anio is said to place his hands beneath her breast, keep her afloat, and share the rights of marriage with her.

records.l: poetry and the liberal arts, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_undervalued wealth and money [in the present age] The narrator asks whether anyone still respects the liberal arts or believes that delicate poetry brings any advantage. He contrasts poetic accomplishment with the military service and wealth that now win social preference.

records.l: the narrator's poems, Heroides and Amores
records.s: The narrator's poems please his lady-love, yet despite her praise, they leave him excluded outside her closed door.

records.l: the newly rich soldier, Heroides and Amores
records.s: A newly rich soldier gains wealth through bloodshed, joins the equestrian order, bears fighting scars, and is preferred to the narrator.

is_preferred_to poetry and the liberal arts [as a means of gaining wealth and status] War is treated as a more profitable pursuit than poetry because it can bring military rank and wealth. The narrator urges the wise to learn to follow battle and organize the foremost spears instead of merely producing good verse.

records.l: wealth and money, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Wealth and money are shown to control love, rank, public office, and social access. The narrator complains that those who can pay command his lady-love and that wealth gives weight to judges and status to knights.

is_a price [the price of Danae's seduction] Gold is described as more powerful than anything else because it can overcome resistance and purchase sexual access. The narrator also says that human beings dig gold from the earth instead of seeking agricultural abundance.
The poor, excluded from the Senate and money’s advantages, are denied love as the rich buy it; the narrator pleads for them to retain something to win.

The rich possess the Campus and Forum and control peace, war, public honors, judgment, and romantic access. The narrator allows them to keep these privileges but objects when their greed takes away the loves of the poor.

explores the sea [beyond what land requires] Human nature is portrayed as ingenious but harmful to itself. It creates fortified cities, weapons, sea travel, and the pursuit of wealth instead of remaining content with the land and its natural gifts.
Nemesis, Tibullus’s recent lover, mourns him at his funeral, kisses him, refuses to leave his pyre, and is imagined accompanying him in Elysium.
Delia, Tibullus’s first love and former beloved, mourns him at his funeral, kisses him with Nemesis and his family, and recalls being happily loved by him.
Bards are called sacred and the care of the gods, and some people believe that they possess divine power. Their work and poetic fame can survive death and fire.

Tibullus’s funeral includes his burning on a pyre and the attendance of his mother, sister, Delia, and Nemesis. His mother closes his dying eyes, his sister shares the grief, and Delia and Nemesis offer kisses before the pyre is left.

records.l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Poetry uniquely survives the pyre, preserving Troy and enduring stories and ensuring Tibullus, Nemesis, and Delia remain known.
At Ceres’s annual festival, honoring Ceres and associated with Egyptian sistrum, the beloved must abstain and sleep separately; the speaker protests love, songs, and wine excluded.

records.l: grain and agriculture, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Ceres teaches grain’s cultivation, harvesting, and plowing with oxen and sickles, replacing acorns and turf herbs; when she leaves for love, crops fail except in fertile Crete.

records.l: Ovid's books of verse, Heroides and Amores
records.s: make_known Corinna [to many readers] Ovid's books of verse have made Corinna known beyond their private relationship. They have therefore helped turn her into a woman who may be shared with many and have harmed Ovid's interests.
Ovid's poetry, stirred by Corinna, publicizes her beauty and freely creates or transmits marvelous myths beyond historical truth.
Halaesus, exiled after Agamemnon’s killing, wanders land and sea, founds Falerii, and teaches its people Juno’s sacred rites.

is_founded_by Halaesus [with auspicious hand] Falerii is associated with an annual festival of Juno involving priestesses, games, processions, offerings, and animal sacrifices. Its Juno rites are said to have been brought by Halaesus, and Ovid wishes the goddess to remain friendly to Falerii and its people.

records.l: love affair and infidelity, Heroides and Amores
records.s: is_the_subject_of Ovid's poetry [in the elegies] Ovid fears that Corinna, formerly regarded as his own, is now involved with many men. He remains attached to her despite jealousy and asks her to continue her affairs privately rather than force him to know or witness them.

records.l: concealment and denial, Heroides and Amores
records.s: Concealment and denial protect public reputation and preserve Ovid’s peace of mind as Corinna is asked to deny visible infidelity, with words overcoming his eyes.

Ovid experiences sexual impotence with a beautiful and willing girl, despite her embraces, kisses, words, and efforts to arouse him. He wonders whether magic, poison, or shame has caused the failure, and contrasts it with his recent success with Chlide, Pitho, Libas, and Corinna.

OVID'S    LIFE 

Publius  Ovidius  Naso  was  born  at  Sulmo,  a  city 
about  ninety  miles  south-east  of  Rome,  in  the  country 
of  the  Paeligni,  on

records.s: about ninety miles south-east of Rome, in the country of the Paeligni, on March 20, 43 B.C., the year of the second triumvirate, composed of Augustus, Antony, and Lepidus, and the year of the proscription and death of the Ciceros. His family had been of equestrian rank for several generations. Ovid's education was begun at Sulmo, and com- pleted at Rome and Athens. In deference to his father's wishes, he pursued, with his brother, the rhetorical studies usual with the ambitious young men of the time, expecting to enter upon a public career ; but so fervent was his passion for literature, and so irresistible his instinct for

records.s: ; but so fervent was his passion for literature, and so irresistible his instinct for literary art — he himself says that whatever he attempted to write took the form of verse — that he found it impossible to follow the profession of his father's preference. He held, indeed, one or two minor offices in the public service, but his chief interests were always among the social and literary circles of the capital. Among those with whom he was intimate were Tibullus, who died when Ovid was twenty-four, Propertius, and Aemilius Macer of Verona. OVID'S LIFE At the age of nineteen, Ovid mourned the death of his only brother. The poet was three times married — twice with divorce as a hasty result, and the third time to a lady of one of the oldest and most respected families of Rome, the Fabii. The last union seems to have been based upon serious affection, or, at least, esteem, and remained un- broken to Ovid's death. A daughter, Perilla, is said to have been born of this marriage. The  Heroides  are  not  a  work  of  the  highest  order 
of  genius.  Their  language,  nearly  always  artificial, 
frequently  rhetorical,  and  often  diffuse,  is  the  same

Medea  or  Sappho  the  poetess.  The  heroin

records.s: whether from the lips of barbarian Medea or Sappho the poetess. The heroines and heroes who speak it are creatures from the world of legend, are not always warm flesh and blood, and rarely communicate their passions to us. The critic who cares more for the raising of a laugh than for the strict rendering of justice may with no great difficulty find room here for the exercise of his wit. Yet the malicious critic of the Heroides will be hard to find ; for they belong to the engaging sort of art which disarms criticism. Their theme, first of all, is the universal theme of love — and of woman's love — and of woman's love in straits. The

What  the  Heroides  lose  by  reason  of  being  the

records.s: HEROIDES What the Heroides lose by reason of being the portrayal of legendary characters in language removed from ordinary life they gain from their pleasant quality of style, and from their constant stimulation of literary reminiscence. They should not be judged as attempts at realistic art ; their author did not aim at even naturalism'. If we must choose, they should be judged on the basis of their connection rather with literature than with life. Yet we need not choose ; we may enjoy them as clever and genial treatments of literary themes enriched with enough of the warmly human to beget in the benevolent reader the illusion of life. Penelope  to  Ulysses 

This  missive  your  Penelope  sends  to  you,  O 
Ulysses,  slow  of  return  that  you  are — yet  write 
nothing  back  to  me  ;  yourself  come  !  Troy,

records.l: Heroides and Amores, P. OVIDI NASONIS HEROIDES / i
records.s: of return that you are — yet write nothing back to me ; yourself come ! Troy, to be sure, is fallen, hated of the daughters of Greece ; but scarcely were Priam and all Troy worth the price to me." O would that then, when his ship was on the way to Lacedaemon, the adulterous lover had been overwhelmed by raging waters ! Then had I not lain cold in my deserted bed, nor would now be left alone complaining of slowly passing days ; nor would the hanging web be wearying now my widowed hands as I seek to beguile the hours of spacious night. 11 When have I not feared dangers graver than the real ?

records.s: I did he tell of how the son of Menoetius fell in armour not his own/' I wept that wiles could lack success. Had Tlepolemus with his blood made warm the Lycian spear,6 in Tlepolemus' fate was all my care renewed. In short, whoever it was in the Argive camp that was pierced and fell, colder than ice grew the heart of her who loves you. 23 But good regard for me had the god who looks with favour upon chaste love. records.s: now, what I am to fear I know not — yet none the less I fear all things, distraught, and wide is the field lies open for my cares. Whatever dangers the deep contains, whatever the land, sus- picion tells me are cause of your long delay. While I live on in foolish fear of things like these, you may be captive to a stranger love — such are the hearts of you men ! It may be you even tell how rustic" a wife you have — one fit only to dress fine the wool. records.s: . Even now my love is loath to let me think you wrong me. Oft have I been false to myself in my defence of you ; oft have I thought the gusty breezes of the south were bringing back your white sails. Theseus I have cursed, because methought he would not let you go; yet mayhap 'tis not he that has stayed your course. At times have I feared lest, while you were holding toward the waters of the Hebrus, your craft had been wrecked and engulfed in the foaming wave. To throw myself hence into the waves beneath has been my mind ; and, since you still pursue your faithless course, so shall it be. Let the waves bear me away, and cast me up on your shores, and let me meet your eyes untombed ! Though in hardness you be more than steel, than adamant, than your very self, you shall say : "

Each, casting eyes into the face of other, inquired in silence where now was the love between us. My going might have been deferred ; a stay of my pain would have eased my heart. All me ! records.s: 'Tis only a tale to me, but to you well known. Reft of her brothers, a mother cursed the hope and head of her son. There was war ; in fierce mood he laid down his arms and stood apart, and with unbending purpose refused his country aid. Only the wife availed to bend her husband. The happier she ! — for my words have no weight, and fall for naught. And yet I am not angered, nor have I borne myself as wife because oft summoned, a slave, to share my master's bed. Though you be cruel, though more savage than your mother's waves, even should I keep silence you will be broken by my tears. 135 Even now — so may Peleus your father fill out his tale of years, so may Pyrrhus take up arms with fortune as good as yours ! — have regard for anxious Briseis, brave Achilles, and do not hard-heartedly torment a wretched maid with long drawn out delay ! Or, if your love for me has turned to weariness, compel the death of her whom you compel to live without you ! And, as you now are doing,

records.s: Phaedra to Hippoi.vtus With wishes for the welfare which she herself, unless you give it hei-, will ever lack, the Cretan maid greets the hero whose mother was an Amazon. Read to the end, whatever is here contained — what shall reading of a letter harm ? In this one, too, there may be something to pleasure you ; in these characters of mine, secrets are borne over land and sea. Even foe looks into missive writ by foe. 7 Thrice making trial of speech with you, thrice hath my tongue vainly stopped, thrice the sound failed at first threshold of my lips. records.s: tortures me. 53 It may be this love is a debt I am paying, due to the destiny of my line, and that Venus is exacting tribute of me for all my race. Europa — this is the first beginning of our line — was loved of Jove ; a bull's form disguised the god. Pasiphae my mother, victim of the deluded bull,* brought forth in travail her reproach and burden. The faithless son of Aegeus followed the guiding thread, and escaped from the winding house through the aid my sister gave." records.s: Here with you will I dwell, in Troezen's land, the realm of Pittheus ; yon place is dearer to me now than my own native soil. The hero son of Neptune is absent now, in happy hour, and will be absent long ; he is kept by the shores of his dear Pirithous."1 Theseus — unless, indeed, we refuse to own what all may see — has come to love Pirithous more than Phaedra, Pirithous more than you. Nor is that the only wrong we suffer at his hand ; there are deep injuries we both have had from him. The bones of my brother he crushed with his triple-knotted club and scattered o'er the ground;

records.s: under name of kinship. Should someone see us embrace, we both shall meet with praise ; I shall be called a faithful stepdame to the son of my lord. No portal of a dour husband will need unbolting for you in the darkness of night; there will be no guard to be eluded ; as the same root' has covered us both, the same will cover us still. Your wont has been to give me kisses unconcealed, your wont will be still to give me kisses unconcealed. My bosom leaped with amaze as you told me of it, and a chill tremor rushed through my hard bones. 1 took counsel — for I was no little terrified — with grandams and long-lived sires. 'Twas clear to us all that evil threatened me. 41 The firs were felled, the timbers hewn ; your fleet was ready, and the deep-blue wave received the waxed crafts. Your tears fell as you left me — this, at least, deny not! We mingled our weeping, each a prey to grief; the elm is not so closely clasped by the clinging vine as was my neck by your embracing arms. records.s: 113 This, once upon a time — for I call it back, to mind — your sister* sang to me, with locks let loose, foreseeing what should come: "What art thou doing, Oenone ? Why commit seeds to sand ? Thou art ploughing the shores with oxen that will accomplish naught. A Greek heifer is on the way, to ruin thee. thy home-land, and thy house ! Ho, keep her far ! A Greek heifer is coming ! While yet ye may, sink in the deep the unclean ship ! Alas, how much of Phrygian blood it hath aboard ! " 121 She ceased to speak ; her slaves seized on her as she madly ran

records.s: " 121 She ceased to speak ; her slaves seized on her as she madly ran. And I — my golden locks stood stiffly up. Ah, all too true a prophetess you were to my poor self — she has them, lo, the heifer has my pastures ! Let her seem how fair soever of face, none the less she surely is a jade ; smitten with a stranger, she left behind her marriage-gods. Theseus — unless I mistake the name — one Theseus, even before, had stolen her away from her father's land.'' Is it to be thought she was rendered back a maid, by a young man and eager? Wrhence have I learned this so well?

Scarce had he well touched the threshold, when I cried, "How doth my lord, the son of Aeson ? " Speechless he stood in embarrassment, his eyes fixed fast upon the ground. I straight leaped up, and rent the garment from my breast. " Lives he?" I cried, "or must fate call me too?" "He lives," was his reply. Full of fears is love ; I made him say it on his oath. records.s: red Argo.rt It flies upon its way; the wind bellies out the sail ; the dark-blue wave glides from under the keel as it drives along ; your gaze is on the land, and mine is on the sea. There is a tower that looks from every side upon the waters round about ; thither I betake myself, my face and bosom wet with tears. Through my tears I gaze ; my eyes are gracious to my eager heart, and see farther than their wont. Add thereto pure-hearted prayers, and vows mingled with fears — vows which I must now fulfil, since you are safe. 75 And am I to absolve these vows — vows but for Medea to

records.s: drives the slender needle — and other deeds 'twere better not to know. Ill sought by herbs is love that should be won by virtue and by beauty. 95 A woman like this can you embrace ? Can you be left in the same chamber with her and not feel fear, and enjoy the slumber of the silent night? Surely, she must have forced you to bear the yoke, just as she forced the bulls, and has you subdued by the same means she uses with fierce dragons. Add that she has her name writ in the record of your own and your heroes' exploits, and the wife obscures the glory of the husband. And someone of the part

And someone of the partisans of Pelias imputes your deeds to her poisons, and wins the people to believe : " This fleece of gold from the ram of Phrixus the son of Aeson did not seize away, but the Phasian girl, Aeetes' child." Your mother Alcimede — ask counsel of your mother — favours her not, nor your sire, who sees his son's bride come from the frozen north. All was grief, everywhere anxiety and fear ; my grandsire wept, and my mother's sister Phoebe, and the twin brothers, and Leda fell to praying the gods above, and her own Jove. records.s: 47 Is this too little for me to endure ? You add to it your stranger loves, and whoever will may be by you a mother. I will say nothing of Aug'e betrayed in the vales of Parthenius, or of thy travail, nymph sprung of Ormenus ; nor will I charge against you the daughters of Teuthras' son, tin- throng of sisters from whose number none was spared by you." But there is one love — a fresh offence of which I have heard — a love by which I am made stepdame to Lydian Lamus.6 The Meander, so many times wandering in the same lands, who oft turns back upon themselves his wearied waters,

Felt you no shame to bind with gold those strong arms, and to set the gem upon that solid brawn ? Ah, to think 'twas these arms that crushed the life from the Nemean pest, whose skin now covers your left side ! You have not shrunk from binding your shaggy hair with a woman's turban ! records.s: IX from laying to the polished wool-basket the hand that triumphed over a thousand toils ; do you draw oft with stalwart thumb the coarsely spun strands, and give back to the hand of a pretty mistress the just portion she weighed out ? Ah, how often, while with dour finger you twisted the thread, have your too strong hands crushed the spindle ! Before your mistress' feet .... and told of the deeds of which you should now say naught — of enormous serpents, throttled and coiling their lengths about your infant hand ; how the Tegeaean boar has his lair on cypress-bearing Erymanthus, and afflicts the ground with his vast weight.

Iole, the daughter of Eurytus, and Aonian Alcides will be basely joined in shameful bonds of Hymen. My mind fails me at the thought, a chill sweeps through my frame, and my hand lies nerveless in my lap. 187 Me, too, you have possessed among vour many loves — but me with no reproach. That you at least might see, it' you could not hear, with might and main I sent you signals with my hands ; and upon a long tree-branch I fixed my shining veil — yes, to put in mind of me those who had forgotten ! With foreboding you depart ; and as you go my moist eyes follow you, and in faint murmur comes from my tongue: "Fare thou well!" Laying myself on the ordered couch within my chamber, grievously wounded, in tears 1 passed the whole night long ; before my eyes appeared the bulls and the dreadful harvest, before my eyes the un- sleeping serpent. I, the maiden who am now at last become a barbarian in your eyes, who now am poor, who now seem baneful — I closed the lids of the flame-like eyes in slumber wrought by my drug, and gave into your hand the fleece to steal away un- harmed. I betrayed my sire, I left my throne and my native soil ; the reward I get is leave to live in exile! My maidenly innocence has become the spoil of a pirate from overseas ; beloved mother and best of sisters I have left behind. 113 But thee, O my brother, I did not leave behind as I fled ! records.s: I did not leave behind as I fled ! In this one place my pen fails. Of the deed my right hand was bold enough to do/' it is not bold enough to write. So I. too, should have been torn limb from limb — but with thee ! And yet I did not fear — for what, after that, could I fear? — to trust myself to the sea, woman though I was, and now with guilt upon me. Where is heavenly justice ? Where the gods? Let the penalty that is our due overtake us on the deep — you for your treachery, me for my trustfulness ! 121 Would the Symplegades had caught and crushed us out

This, too, moves me, that the winds forbid your keels to fare forth — yet you make readyr to sail despite the seas. Who would be willing to return homeward with the wind saying nay ? Yet you trim sail to leave your homes, though the sea forbids! Neptune himself will open up no way for you against his own city. Whither your headlong course? Return ye all to your own abodes! XIV Hypermnesxra to Lvnceus Hypermnestra sends this letter to the one brother left of so many but now alive — the rest of the company lie dead by the crime of their brides. Kept close in the palace am I, bound with heavy chains; and the cause of my punishment is that I was faithful. Because my hand shrank from driving into your throat the steel, I am charged with crime ; I should be praised, had I but dared the deed. records.s: now, heavy with food and wine they lay in sleep, and deep repose had settled on Argns, free from care — when round about me I seemed to hear the groans of dying men; nay, I heard indeed. and what I feared was true. My blood retreated, warmth left my body and soul, and on my newly- wedded couch all chill I lav. As the gentle zephyr sets a-quiver the slender stalk of grain, as wintry breezes shake the poplar leaves, even thus— yea, even more — did I tremble. records.s: me to death, and, when my body is done with life, lay it in secret on the funeral pile, and bury my bones moistened with faithful tears, and let my sepulchre be graved with this brief epitaph : " Exiled Hyper- mnestra, as the unjust price of her wifely deed, has herself endured the death she warded from her brother!" 131 1 would wi*ite more ; but my hand falls with the weight of my chains, and very fear takes away my strength. records.s: from my eager right hand, did your eye know forth- with whose they were — or, unless you had read their author's name, Sappho, would you fail to know whence these brief words come ? 5 Perhaps, too, you may ask why my verses alter- nate, when I am better suited to the lyric mode. I must weep, for my love — and elegy is the weeping strain ; no lyre is suited to my tears. 9 I burn — as burns the fruitful acre when its harvests are ablaze, with untamed cast-winds driving on the flame. The fields you frequent, O Phaon, lie far away, by Typhoean Aetna ; and I — heat

records.s: not in Atthis as once they did, nor in the hundred other maids I loved here to my reproach ; unworthy one, the love that belonged to many maids you alone possess. 21 You have beauty, and your years are apt for life's delights — O beauty that lay in ambush for my eyes ! Take up the lyre and quiver — you will be Apollo manifest ; let horns but spring on your head • — you will be Bacchus ! Phoebus loved Daphne, and Bacchus, too, loved the Gnosian maid, and neither one nor other knew the lyric mode ; yet for me the daughters of Pegasus dictate sweetest songs ; my name is already sung abroad in

records.s: me the daughters of Pegasus dictate sweetest songs ; my name is already sung abroad in all the earth. Not greater is the praise Alcaeus wins, the sharer in my homeland and in my gift of song, though a statelier strain he sounds. If nature, malign to me, has denied the charm of beauty, weigh in the stead of beauty the genius she gave. I am slight of stature, yet I have a name fills every land ; the measure of my name is my real height. records.s: My kisses too you praised, and I pleased in every way — but then above all when we wrought at the task of love. Then did my playful ways delight you more than your wont — the quick embrace, the jest that gave spice to our sport, and, when the joys of both had mingled into one, the deep, deep languor in our wearied frames. 51 Now new prey is yours — the maids of Sicily. What is Lesbos now to me ? I would I were a Sicilian maid.*1 Ah, send me back my wanderer, ye Nisaean matrons and Nisaean maids, nor let the lies of his bland tongue deceive you ! What he sav

records.s: maids, nor let the lies of his bland tongue deceive you ! What he savs to you, he had said before to me. Thou too, Erycina, who dost frequent the Sicanian mountains — for I am thine — protect thy singer, O lady ! Can it be my grievous fortune will hold the ways it first began, and ever remain bitter in its course ? Six natal days had passed for me, when I gathered the bones of my father, dead before his time, and let them drink my tears. My untaught brother was caught in the flame of harlot love, and suffered loss together with foul shame ; reduced to need, he roams the dark blue seas

But how much better for my bosom to be pressed to yours than headlong to be hurled from the rocks ! — the bosom, Phaon, of her whom you were wont to praise, and who so often seemed to you to have the gift of genius. Would I were eloquent now ! Grief stops my art, and all my genius is halted by my woes. My old-time power in song will not respond to the call ; my plectrum for grief is silent ; mute for grief is my lyre. records.s: has driven me hither, nor a wandering course ; Taenaris is the land toward which inv ships were steered. Nor think I cleave the seas with a keel that carries merchandise — what goods I have, may the gods only keep for me ! Nor am I come as one to see the sights of Grecian towns — the cities of my own realm are wealthier. It is you I come for — you, whom golden Venus has promised for my bed; you were my heart's desire before you were known to me. Jove's consort loudly offers thrones, his daughter, might in war ; I myself waver, and can make no choice between power and the valorous heart. The son, after long time, is taken back to his home, the house is glad, and Troy adds this day, too, to its festivals. And as I long for you, so women have longed for me ; alone, you can possess the object of many women's prayers ! And not only have the daughters of princes and chieftains sought me, but even the nymphs have felt for me the cares of love. Whose beauty was I to admire more than Oenone's ? — after you

But I am weary of all of them, Tyndaris, since hope was made mine of winning you. It was you that rilled my vision as I waked, and you my sold saw in the night, when eyes lie overcome in peaceful slumber. What will you be face to face, you who won me yet unseen ? I was fired with love, though here, far away, was the flame. I could not longer cheat myself of the hope of you, but started on the dark blue path

A truthful prophetess was she ; I have found the fires of which she spoke, and flames of fierce love rage in my helpless breast ! 127 I sail forth from the harbour, and with favour- ing winds disembark upon your shores, O nymph of Oebalus' line. Your lord receives me as befits a guest — this, too, an act not without the counsel and approval of the gods ! He showed me, of course, whatever in all Lacedaemon was worthy to be shown and sightly to be seen

A Phrygian, too, Anchises, with whom the mother of the winged loves rejoices to consort on Ida's ridge. I shall at least not give you a father-in-law who puts to flight the clear beams of the sun, and turns away from the feast his affrighted steeds ; b nor has Priam a sire, who is stained with blood from the murder of bis bride

Ah, too simple — nay, too rustic — Helen ! do you think that beauty of yours can be free from fault ? Either you must change your beauty, or you must needs not be hard ; fairness and modesty are mightily at strife. Jove's delight, and the delight of Venus, are in stealthy sins like these ; such stealthy sins, indeed, gave you Jove for sire. Your beauty, too, I confess, is rare, and a woman might well wish to submit to your embrace ; but let another be happy without reproach rather than my honour fall before a stranger's love. Learn from my example how to live without the fair ; there is virtue in abstinence from what delights. How many youths, think you, desire what you desire, and yet are wise ? Or are you, Paris, the only one with eyes ? You see no more clearly : your daring is only more rash ; nor have you more spirit, but less of modesty. 231 OVID Tunc ego te

records.l: Heroides and Amores, Prima mea est igitur Veneri plaeuisse voluptas ;
records.s: I seemed the greatest prize to you, and that you placed first the honours neither of Pallas nor of Juno when you had heard of Helen's parts. So, then, I mean valour to you, I mean a far-famed throne ! I should be of iron, did I not love such a heart. Of iron, believe me, I am not ; but I fight against my love for one who I think can hardly become my own. Why should I essay with curved plough to furrow the watery shore, and to follow a hope which the place itself denies ? I am not practised in the theft of love, and never yet — the gods are my witnesses —

" And straight the strength came back to my wearied arms, and the wave seemed easier to me than before. To keep me from the chill of the cold deep, love lends his aid, hot in my eager breast. The nearer I approach, and the nearer draw the shores, and the less of the way remains, the greater my joy to hasten on. When in truth I can be seen as well as see, by your glance you straightway give me heart, and make me strong. Now, too, I strain in my course to pleasure

Against the wish of my heart I regain my own land — who could believe ? Against the wish of my heart I tarry now in my own town. 125 Ah me ! why are we joined in soul and parted by the wave ; two beings of one mind, but not of one land ? Either let your Sestos take me, or my Abydos you ; your land is as dear to me as mine is dear to you. Why must my heart be troubled as oft as the sea is troubled ?

And, lest you deem I promise this because the time is not yet come, I will give you no tardy pledge of what I promise. Let the sea be swollen still for these few nights, and I shall essay to cross despite the waves ; either happy daring shall leave me safe, or death shall be the end of my anxious love ! records.s: "To-morrow," she says, " we shall be more," and herself drinks of the wine. Ah, do make us mure, glide over the conquered wave, O you whom I have welcomed to all my inmost heart ! Come back to camp, deserter of your ally love ; why must I lay my limbs in the mid space of my couch ? There is naught for you to fear ! Venus' self will smile upon your venture ; child of the sea, the paths of the sea she will make smooth. Oft am I prompted myself to go through the midst of the waves, but 'tis the wont of this strait to be safer for men. For why,

For why, though Phrixus and Phrixus' sister both rode this way, did the maiden alone give name to these wide waters? 165 Perhaps you fear the time may fail you for return, or you may not endure the effort of the twofold toil. Then let us both from diverse ways come together in mid sea, and give each other kisses on the waters' crest, and so return again each to his own town ; 'twill be little, but more than naught ! Would that either this shame that compels us to secret loving would cease, or else the love that fears men's speech. Now,

records.s: you swim. 181 Yet, O my young lover, though victor over the swollen waters, so spurn the sea as still to be in fear of it ! Ships wrought with skill are over- whelmed by the wave ; do you think your arms more powerful than oars ? What you are eager for, Leander — to swim — is the sailor's fear ; 'tis that follows ever on the wreck of ships. Ah, wretched me ! I am eager not to persuade you to what I urge ; may you be too strong, I pray, to yield to my admonition — only so you come to me, and cast about my neck the wearied arms oft beaten by the wave ! 191

She was there, and, present as she was, marked your words, and seemed, by the shaking of her locks, to have accepted them. 21 I will give you leave to say you were deceived, and by wiles of mine, if only of those wiles my love be counted cause. What was the object of my wiles but the one thing — to be united with you ? The thing you complain of has power to join you to me. Neither by nature nor by practice am I so cunning ; believe me, maid, it is you who make me skilful. It was ingenious Love who bound you to me,

records.s: 107 Alas me ! Cydippe, I fear to tell you the truth, lest I seem to warn you falsely, for the sake of my plea ; yet tell it I must. This is the reason, believe me, why you oft lie ill on the eve of marriage.6 It is the goddess herself, looking to your good, and striving to keep you from a false oath ; she wishes you kept whole by the keeping whole of your faith. This is the reason why, as oft as you attempt to break your oath, she corrects your sin. Cease to invite forth the cruel bow of the spirited virgin ; she still may be appeased, if only you allow.

records.s: And now I feel an added fear, lest someone besides the nurse who shares my secret may see that we are interchanging words. She sits before the door, and when they ask how I do within, answers, "She sleeps," that I may write in safety. Presently, when sleep, the excellent excuse for my long retreat, no longer wins belief because I tarry so, and now she sees those coming whom not to admit is hard, she clears her throat and thus gives me the sign agreed upon. I already am shamed, and in fear, though I feel no guilt within, lest I appear to have merited the displeasure of the gods. One contends that my affliction is the work of chance ; another says that my destined husband finds not favour with the gods ; and, lest you think yourself untouched by what men say, there are also some who think you the cause, by poisonous arts. Their source is hidden, but my ills are clear to see ; you two stir up fierce strife and banish peace, and the blows are mine ! 55 Tell me

At mention of the name of wedlock I was confused and shamed, and felt the blushes cover all my face, and my eyes I kept upon my bosom as if fastened there — those eyes that were made ministers to your intent. Wretch, why rejoice ? or what glory have you gained ? or what praise have you won, a man, by playing on a maid ? I did not present myself before you with buckler and axe in hand, like a Penthesilea on the soil of Ilion ; no sword-girdle, chased with Amazonian gold, was offered you for spoil by me, as by some Hippolyte.0 Why exult if your words

Already have I wearied enough with the pen my weakened members, and my sick hand refuses longer its office. records.s: like this, and has made my body apt thereto by wasting away my flesh. Love it is that teaches me how to walk softly past the watchful guard ; love is the guide that keeps my steps from stumbling. 9 Yet once I was ever in fear of the night and its empty phantoms ; I marvelled at whosoever would venture abroad in darkness. Whenever she has willed, the clouds are rolled together over all the sky ; whenever she has willed, the day shines forth in a clear heaven. IX Every lover is a soldier, and Cupid has a camp of his own ; Atticus, believe me, every lover is a soldier. The age that is meet for the wars is also suited to Venus. 'Tis unseemly for the old man to soldier, unseemly for the old man to love. The spirit that captains seek in the valiant soldier is the same the fair maid seeks in the man who mates with her. records.s: OHES I. xi the stealthy night and skilled in the giving of the signal, oft urging Corinna when in doubt to come to me, often found tried and true to me in times of trouble — receive and take early to your mistress these tablets I have inscribed, and care that nothing hinder or delay ! Your breast has in it no vein of Hint or unyielding iron, nor ai-e you simpler than befits your station. One could believe you, too, had felt the darts of Cupid — in aiding me defend the standards of your own campaigns ! Should she ask how I fare, you will say 'tis my hope of her favour that lets me live ; as for

records.s: you ! Yea, and the man who converted you from a tree to an' object for use, I will assure you, did not have pure hands. That tree, too, lent itself to the hanging of some wretched neck, and furnished the cruel cross to the executioner; it gave its foul shade to hoarse horned owls, and its branches bore up the eggs of the screech-owl and the vulture. To tablets like these did I insanely commit my loves and give my tender words to be carried to my lady ? records.s: comb. The hair-dresser's person was ever safe ; oft has my love's toilet been made before my eyes, and she never snatched up hairpin to wound her servant's arms. Often, too, in early morning when her hair was not yet dressed, she has lain half supine on her purple couch. Even then, in her neglect, she was comely, like a Thracian Bacchante lying careless and wearied on the green turf. 23 And yet, seeing they were delicate and like to down, alas, what woes were theirs, and what tortures they endured ! No rival's enchanted herbs have wrought you ill, no treacherous grandam has laved your hair with water from Haemonian land ; b nor has violent illness harmed — far from us he the omen ! — nor envious tongue diminished your dense locks. The loss you feel was wrought you by your own hand and fault ; yourself applied the mingled poison to your head. 45 Now Germany will send you tresses from captive women ; you will be adorned by the bounty of the race we lead in triumph. records.s: multa superstes erit. 378 THE AMORES I. xv rugged in art, and Accius of the spirited tongue, possess names that will never fade. Varro and the first of ships — what generation will fail to know of them, and of the golden fleece, the Aesonian chieftain's quest ? The verses of sublime Lucretius will perish only then when a single day shall give the earth to doom. Tityrus and the harvest, and the arms of Aeneas, will be read as long as Rome shall be capital of the world she triumphs o'er ; as long as flames and bow are the arms of Cupid, thy numbers shall be conned, O elegant Tibullus

But a tender beloved, at my oft praising of her beauty has come of herself to the poet as the reward for his song. Great is my recompense ! Renowned names of heroes, fare ye well ; your favours are not the kind for me ! And fair ones, turn hither your beauteous faces as I sing the songs which rosy Love dictates to me ! He is one favoured, and rules in the house, and feels no blows ; he is one with power — the rest, a mean crowd, are at his feet. For the husband empty reasons are fashioned to keep the true ones hid ; and both master and mistress approve what the mistress alone approves. records.s: Juno's watchman, guarding lo too intently, falls before his time ; she — becomes a goddess ! I have seen in shackles the livid legs of a man who had forced a husband to know himself a cuckold. The punishment was less than he deserved. His evil tongue brought harm to two ; the hus- band suffered grief, the wife the loss of her good name. Believe me, accusations are welcome to no husband, nor do they please him, even though he hear. If he is cool, you bring your traitorous tales to careless ears ; if he loves, your service only makes him wretched. 55 Nor is a fault, however manifest, an easy thing to prove

records.s: Readily would you be compliant and yielding to lovers' prayers, if you had ever grown warm with love for any woman. You were not born for a horse, nor for the strenuous service of arms ; the warlike spear fits noj your right hand. Let men engage in those ways of life ; do you lay aside all manly hopes. The standards you bear must be of your mistress's service. Whether 'tis some fair one with modest eyes downcast upon her lap, I am aflame, and that innocence is my ensnaring ; whether 'tis some saucy jade, I am smitten because she is not rustic simple, and gives me hope of enjoying her supple embrace on the soft couch. If she seem austere, and affects the rigid Sabine dame, I judge she would yield, but is deep in her deceit. records.s: the downfall of the guilty. 13 I saw your guilty acts my wretched self with sober eye, when the wine had been placed and you thought I slept. I saw you both say many things with quiverings of the brow ; in your nods was much of speech. Your eyes, too, girl, were not dumb, and the table was written o'er with wine, nor did any letter fail your fingers. Your speech, too, I recognized was busied with hidden message, and your words charged to stand for certain meanings. records.s: ORES II. VI Our parrot, winged mimic from Indian land of dawn, is no more — come flocking, ye birds, to his obsequies ! Come, all ye feathered faithful, come beat your breasts with the wing, and mark your tender cheeks with the rigid claw ; let your ruffled plumage be rent in place of mourning hair, and in place of the long trumpet let your songs sound out ! If you, Philomela, are lamenting the deed of the tyrant of Ismarus,a that lament has been fulfilled bv its term of years ; turn aside to the hapless funeral of no common bird — great cause for grief is Itys, but belongs to the ancient

records.s: tis the cause of their often living to old-wives' age. You were sated with very little ; speech you loved so well that your beak had no time for many foods. A nut was your fare, and poppy-seeds brought you sleep, and drops of unmixed water drove away your thirst. records.s: Hein. 412 THE AMORES II. x maids at once. Each one is beautiful, both taste- ful in their dress ; in accomplishment, 'tis doubtful whether the one or the other is first. The one is fairer than the other — and the other is also fairer than she ; one pleases me the more — and so does the other, too ! Like a yacht that is driven by contrary winds, my love is now for the one and now for the other ; it veers about, and keeps me torn in two. Why, O lady of Eryx, dost thou double endlessly my woes ? Was not one love enough to keep me anxious ? Why add leaves to the

Why add leaves to the trees, stars to a full sky, and heaped-up waters to the deep seas? 15 And yet 'tis better thus than if I were loveless and alone — to my enemies fall the austere life ! To my enemies fall the lot of sleep in a lonely bed, and the laying their limbs loosely in its midst. But for me — let cruel love break off my lazy slumbers, and may I not be the only burden of my bed ! Let my powers be waste by love, and no one say me nay — if one suffices, well ; if not, then two ! Corinna flies from the couch that knows her, and the Penates she has shared', and makes ready to venture forth on treacherous paths. Why, ah. wretched me ! — must I fear for you the West- wind and the East, and frozen Boreas, and the balmy South ? Xot yonder will you gaze on towns, not upon groves ; there is only the deep-blue form of the unjust sea. Nor do the waters in the mid of the deep have delicate shells and painted pebbles ; for those we linger on the thirsty strand. Print ye the strand with marble-white feet

And let others tell you tales of battling winds ; of waters that Scvlla makes dread, or Charybdis ; of rocks where the violent Ceraunians tower from the sea ; of the fold in the shore where the Syrtes, great and lessor, lie in wait. These things let others tell you ; whatever each shall say, believe it!
